title: The Devotee Prince

full_text:
Prince Harun, a royal prince of the Abbasid dynasty, grew weary of the luxury, flattering courtiers, and political intrigues of the Baghdad court. Realizing that worldly crowns cannot satisfy the longing of the soul, he abandoned his palace by night, donned a coarse woollen tunic, and traveled down the river to the bustling port city of Basra.

There, among the docks and brickyards, he hired himself out as a simple day-laborer, working every Saturday as a mason’s assistant, carrying heavy mortar and bricks up high scaffolds.

He had one peculiar rule: he worked only on Saturdays, earned exactly one dirham and a single copper fals, and refused to labor for the rest of the week, spending his days in contemplation, study, and prayer in the great mosque. The one dirham he spent on barley bread and water, and the copper coin he gave to the poor.

The master builder of Basra marveled at his worker: 'This young laborer works with such quiet diligence and flawless honesty that he accomplishes in one day what three ordinary men cannot finish in a week, yet he refuses to take a single coin more than his simple need.'

After several years, the young prince fell ill of a fever. Lying upon a simple palm mat in a modest hut, he sent for the master builder and handed him a sealed ring bearing the royal crest of the Caliph of Baghdad.

'When I depart,' whispered the youth, 'take this ring to the Commander of the Faithful, and tell him: "Your brother has returned to his Creator, possessing nothing of this world save a clear conscience and the joy of honest labor."'

When the Caliph received the ring, he wept bitterly, acknowledging that his humble brother had conquered a greater kingdom with his mason’s trowel than all the armies of Baghdad could ever subdue with the sword.
moral: Inner peace earned by honest manual labor is more noble than all the gilded trappings of royal palaces.

Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
